articles.title: Clippers slam NBA probe as 'witch hunt,' vow to explore 'every legal remedy to address this gross injustice'
articles.summary: The NBA dropped the hammer on the Los Angeles Clippers and team owner Steve Ballmer on Wednesday, and the Clippers vowed to fight back.
articles.body:
The NBA dropped the hammer on the Los Angeles Clippers and team owner Steve Ballmer on Wednesday, and the Clippers are vowing to fight back.

The league released the long-awaited results of its investigation into allegations that the Clippers circumvented the NBA's salary cap in its dealings with All-Star Kawhi Leonard and multiple third-party vendors.

The league concluded that the Clippers and Leonard did circumvent the salary cap and handed down discipline to multiple parties. Among the disciplinary actions, the NBA stripped the Clippers of five first-round draft picks, fined Ballmer $30 million and issued Ballmer a one-year ban "from all league and team activities."

Leonard was fined $700,000 for what the league determined was his role in the scandal.

For the discipline of Ballmer and the Clippers, the team issued two impassioned statements Wednesday in defiance of the NBA's findings and its disciplinary measures.

Clippers reject 'heavily biased investigation'

The first, unsigned, "vehemently" rejected the league's findings, which the team vowed to "rigorously challenge."

"We vehemently reject the NBA's findings, which are the result of a heavily biased investigation seeking to justify a predetermined narrative rather than facts and evidence," the statement reads. "What the league told us privately differs from what it announced today publicly, and they have not held themselves close to the standard Commissioner Silver set at the start of this investigation to ensure its fairness and accuracy. "For the past year, we cooperated fully and in good faith and we will now fight just as hard to demonstrate our innocence. We intend to vigorously challenge these findings and penalties through every avenue available to us and look forward to an ethical and impartial arbitration process."

"We vehemently reject the NBA's findings, which are the result of a heavily biased investigation seeking to justify a predetermined narrative rather than facts and evidence," the statement reads. "What the league told us privately differs from what it announced today publicly, and they have not held themselves close to the standard Commissioner Silver set at the start of this investigation to ensure its fairness and accuracy.

"For the past year, we cooperated fully and in good faith and we will now fight just as hard to demonstrate our innocence. We intend to vigorously challenge these findings and penalties through every avenue available to us and look forward to an ethical and impartial arbitration process."

Also Wednesday, the team issued a letter addressed to NBA commissioner Adam Silver detailing its issues with the league's investigation, which it called a "witch hunt."

The letter signed by Clippers attorney David N. Kelley slammed the scope of the investigation and repeatedly belittled the source that sparked the probe, a Pulitzer Prize-winning investigation by the "Pablo Torre Finds Out" podcast .

The letter was not signed by Ballmer, who has not issued a personal response to the league's discipline. But it certainly represented him while claiming that Ballmer "spent nearly $50 million" to fund the probe that was run by independent law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz . It stated that Ballmer "reimbursed the costs of at least six law firms, many of which were hired at the demands of the league's lawyers."

The letter contends that the investigation has "permanently strained relationships with key Clippers stakeholders" and that "Mr. Ballmer's reputation has been irreparably damaged" in this "heavily biased investigation." It goes on to slam the "podcaster's baseless claims."

The letter reiterated the Clippers' contention that the NBA told them one thing about the investigation in private before producing an entirely different conclusion via the investigation and league announcement issued Wednesday.

"League counsel has acknowledged in our discussions that the league does not believe there was an agreement between the Clippers and Aspiration to funnel money to Kawhi Leonard," the letter reads. "… Nonetheless, with less than an hour's warning, and no opportunity to respond, the league has issued a report and accompanying press release purporting to conclude the exact opposite of what it has said privately."

The letter maintains the Clippers' contention that they did nothing wrong in introducing Leonard to team vendors, which the league says acted as third-party funnels to send tens of millions of dollars to Leonard from the Clippers in circumvention of the salary cap.

The letter concludes with a vow to fight the findings of the investigation and the resulting discipline:

"This investigation has been flawed from the outset. And your decision to issue this report without any notice to the Clippers or their counsel is inexcusable. "This type of witch hunt flies in the face of fundamental fairness and the integrity of the league and of this sport that we all love. We are exploring every legal remedy to address this gross injustice."

"This investigation has been flawed from the outset. And your decision to issue this report without any notice to the Clippers or their counsel is inexcusable.

"This type of witch hunt flies in the face of fundamental fairness and the integrity of the league and of this sport that we all love. We are exploring every legal remedy to address this gross injustice."

The Clippers' avenues to fight the findings might be limited. In announcing its findings, the league stated that the discipline had been agreed upon with the players' union and is "final and binding on all parties."

A source told NBA insider Marc Stein that the Clippers have no route within NBA bylaws to contest the investigations or discipline and will have to seek other legal avenues.

In its findings, the league states that it has evidence that the Clippers facilitated third-party deals between Leonard and their vendors and "induced the companies to enter into these agreements by offering them business from the team."

Citing email exchanges involving executives from a vendor working with the Clippers, the 35-page report by Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz goes into detail of how those dealings allegedly went down.

Per the report, Joseph Sanberg, the co-founder of Aspiration and now a convicted felon on fraud charges, approached Aspiration executives about a four-year, $48 million endorsement deal for Leonard. Aspiration is a now-defunct third-party vendor that was at the heart of the league's probe.

When those executives scoffed at the proposed Leonard deal as financially irresponsible, Sanberg responded thusly, per the report:

When these concerns were conveyed to Mr. Sanberg, he told the Aspiration executives that "the Clippers are asking us to do this with Kawhi Leonard" and that the team would provide additional business back to Aspiration to help offset the financial impact on Aspiration. In an email exchange among Aspiration's CEO, CFO, and general counsel, one wrote, "[Mr. Sanberg said] that the Clippers are promising to increase the amount they pay us per quarter in line with what we pay this guy [i.e., Mr. Leonard]." Another responded: "Thanks for verifying. . . . We should be fine if it's cashflow neutral."

In an email exchange among Aspiration's CEO, CFO, and general counsel, one wrote, "[Mr. Sanberg said] that the Clippers are promising to increase the amount they pay us per quarter in line with what we pay this guy [i.e., Mr. Leonard]." Another responded: "Thanks for verifying. . . . We should be fine if it's cashflow neutral."

What's next for the Clippers isn't clear. But it's evident that this saga is not over.

articles.title: 5 takeaways from the NBA's punishment of the Clippers: By dropping a sledgehammer, Adam Silver squares off against the league's richest owner
articles.summary: Here are five takeaways in the aftermath of the NBA's punishment of the Los Angeles Clippers.
articles.body:
Adam Silver didn't just drop the hammer on the Los Angeles Clippers. He busted out the sledgehammer and called in the wrecking ball for good measure.

Make no mistake about it, the commissioner sent a message on Wednesday. Not just to the Clippers. He cc'd the entire NBA and anyone who dared to think about the words, "cap circumvention."

Among the league's punishments to the Clippers after an investigation found that they broke league rules in order to pay Kawhi Leonard under the table: a $30 million fine; the loss of five first-round picks beginning in 2029; one-year suspensions for owner Steve Ballmer and top business executive Gillian Zucker; and a six-month suspension for top basketball executive Lawrence Frank. The team will also be subject to a compliance and monitoring program for the next five years.

For his part in the scheme, Leonard will be fined $700,000 and his former representative, Dennis Robertson, will be banned from league business activities for five years.

Leonard and Robertson will be fine. This was all about punishing Ballmer, the richest owner in sports, and hitting him where it hurts.

Here are my five takeaways in the aftermath of Wednesday's news.

1. Steve Ballmer has two strikes. Next one, he will be out.

Don't forget, this isn't the first time Ballmer has been punished for cap circumvention. In 2015, the NBA fined the Clippers $250,000 for breaking league rules by offering an impermissible endorsement deal for DeAndre Jordan in free agency. Obviously, Ballmer didn't learn his lesson.

Silver and his lawyers had to have known that any monetary punishment wasn't going to change Ballmer's ways. Indeed, the former Microsoft mogul won't lose a minute of sleep over the monetary hit. A $30 million fine for someone worth $150 billion (Forbes estimates $152.7 billion, to be exact) is the equivalent of a $200 fine for someone worth $1 million. The money was never going to be the deterrent in something like this.

Yes, losing the five first-round picks will hurt basketball operations, for sure. But the thing that will hurt Ballmer and the Clippers the most?

It's Ballmer's one-year ban. That pain has nothing to do with basketball or money. That has to do with power. Silver locked the king out of his castle. Which, as commissioner, is well within his right. In 2000, David Stern, Silver's predecessor and mentor, also banned Minnesota Timberwolves owner Glen Taylor for a year for cap circumvention regarding free agent Joe Smith.

Silver took a page out of Stern's book and did what many around the league didn't think he would do: He stood up to the owner he famously ushered into the NBA in the first place and told him in no uncertain terms that no owner is bigger than the league.

That one-year ban, above all else, is what will dissuade other owners and executives from engaging in cap circumvention. If he did it to Ballmer …

Ballmer is not happy with the verdict and you can tell from the team's official statement issued moments after the news broke:

We vehemently reject the NBA's findings, which are the result of a heavily biased investigation seeking to justify a predetermined narrative rather than facts and evidence. What the league told us privately differs from what it announced today publicly, and they have not held themselves close to the standard Commissioner Silver set at the start of this investigation to ensure it's [sic] fairness and accuracy. For the past year, we cooperated fully and in good faith and we will now fight just as hard to demonstrate our innocence. We intend to vigorously challenge these findings and penalties through every avenue available to us and look forward to an ethical and impartial arbitration process.

We vehemently reject the NBA's findings, which are the result of a heavily biased investigation seeking to justify a predetermined narrative rather than facts and evidence. What the league told us privately differs from what it announced today publicly, and they have not held themselves close to the standard Commissioner Silver set at the start of this investigation to ensure it's [sic] fairness and accuracy.

For the past year, we cooperated fully and in good faith and we will now fight just as hard to demonstrate our innocence. We intend to vigorously challenge these findings and penalties through every avenue available to us and look forward to an ethical and impartial arbitration process.

We're all waiting for that. We've been waiting for a year. Ever since Pablo Torre broke the story about Kawhi Leonard's no-show contract with Aspiration on Sept. 3, 2025, the public has been waiting for something — anything — to justify all of the reported under-the-table dealings and clear the air. I fully recommend watching the now FOURTEEN-part investigation with Torre, Amin Elhassan and David Samson on Pablo Torre Finds Out, for which they've already won a Pulitzer Prize for audio reporting.

In its initial response to PTFO, the Clippers said the allegations of cap circumvention were "provably false." The NBA evidently determined otherwise. Ballmer sat down for an ESPN interview last September and said he was conned. The NBA evidently determined otherwise.

By dropping the sledgehammer and wrecking ball on the Clippers, the NBA evidently found PTFO's investigation to be credible and Ballmer's testimony on ESPN in early September to be incredibly dubious, if not downright deceitful. The published 35-page investigation summary by Wachtell, Lipton, Rozen and Katz law firm outlines plenty of documentation and behaviors that directly contradict Ballmer's assertion that he and the Clippers were innocent of any wrongdoing. Among the many details the investigation uncovered: the finding that the Clippers were paying out millions of dollars worth of "consulting fees" to third parties once they inked endorsement deals with Leonard, companies he never publicly endorsed.

Silver banning Ballmer for a year should be considered way more punitive than Taylor's one-year ban. Taylor wasn't demonstrably beating his chest during games yelling like a diehard fan. He wasn't on the Jumbotron and the TV screen throughout the games. Taylor wasn't sitting courtside with President Barack Obama and Bill Gates as his guests.

Now that Mark Cuban sold his majority stake in the Dallas Mavericks, Ballmer may be the most active and front-facing NBA owner in the game. Ballmer was very much part of the Clippers product, and he made himself a part of it, front and center. Silver and the NBA knew that in its adjudication and still went forward with it.

The NBA didn't cross the Donald Sterling line and ban Ballmer for life like it did with the disgraced previous owner in 2014. But if Ballmer attempts to circumvent the cap a third time, my belief is Silver will have no choice but to remove him as an owner. Read between the lines in Wednesday's punishment and it's hard to see it happening any other way.

2. This is a big win for the integrity of the league

From a legal sense, the 2025-26 season was a nightmare for the NBA.

Less than two months after the Kawhi scandal erupted, the NBA was shook to its core by the FBI announcing federal indictments for illegal sports gambling and poker activity involving Hall of Famer Chauncey Billups and former NBA player and coach Damon Jones as part of a wide-ranging, far-reaching scheme that named 31 defendants. NBA players Terry Rozier and Malik Beasley are also ensnared in the FBI's web. Billups, Rozier and Beasley have all maintained their innocence and await trial while Jones and many others have pleaded guilty.

Beyond the gambling scandal — which should absolutely not be tossed aside lightly — the Aspiration scandal stood as Silver's biggest pressure test of power. Speaking for myself as a media member, the Kawhi Leonard investigation was the topic du jour amongst journalists and insiders at every NBA gathering over the past year. Questions hung over the league throughout the season, including NBA All-Star Weekend in Ballmer's building, Intuit Dome. Would Silver have the stomach to hold Ballmer accountable? Would the league's independent investigation into the richest owner be legit?

At the heart of it all: Can we trust the NBA to do the right thing?

The immediate reaction in the NBA world was a resounding yes. At least in this case. The NBA could have let Ballmer skirt the rules and get away with it. The organization certainly believes it should have gotten off scot free. But given the mountains of evidence (literally piles of it on Torre's desk), the NBA felt Ballmer and the team's illegal actions were beyond the pale.

With the Donaghy scandal that rocked the NBA two decades ago and the ongoing gambling scandals amid sportsbook business ties, the league was in danger of facing an integrity crisis that would cripple the league. The Ballmer punishment was Silver's way of saying that the rules are there for a reason. Break them at your own peril. Even if you're worth more money than just about every NBA owner combined.

As a media member and fan of the game, I'm glad the league is attempting to uphold the integrity of the game. It's all we have.

3. Kawhi Leonard could win a title this year

Just for kicks, Leonard's statement should be read side-by-side to the Clippers. Ballmer's team issued a fiery response and seemed to be threatening legal action against the NBA by saying they're going to fight "through every avenue available to us."

Meanwhile, Leonard owned up to it, accepted the punishment and went on his way. Presumably, the Toronto trade will now be finalized (Kawhi said "As I return to Toronto …") and the former NBA Finals MVP will join Scottie Barnes in a quest to bring Canada its second NBA title.

The Raptors should be thrilled with this ruling. Leonard was not suspended and they don't have to deal with the Uncle Dennis headaches anymore, which is no small thing. Remember, the Raptors reported Robertson's illegal asks to the league back in 2019 and the league decided not to levy any punishments on Leonard then. Now, they get Leonard following an All-NBA season in which I rated him as a top-five player.

The Raptors are going to be a nasty foe next season. Under coach Darko Rajaković, the feisty team finished 10 games above .500 last season armed with the sixth-best defense in the NBA. The defense didn't hold up in the postseason as the Cleveland Cavaliers' starpower took out the Raptors in Game 7. Oh, the Raptors need starpower? Enter the best player in team history, Kawhi Leonard.

Granted, Leonard may succumb to Father Time as he enters his age-35 season. The knee issues could bark up again. But the upside is worth the risk. Not only has there been a new NBA champion in each of the past eight years, but that's also true for the Eastern Conference champ over that same time. The Raptors know this history very well. The team to break up the Cavaliers' four-year reign atop the East in 2019 was the Raptors themselves.

The Raptors are a longshot, to be sure. As of Wednesday night, after the punishment, BetMGM has Toronto currently listed at +3000, tied with the Detroit Pistons and Miami Heat for ninth-most likely team to hoist the Larry O'Brien Trophy in 2027. Crazier things have happened. Like, say, Adam Silver banning Steve Ballmer.

OK, now to the basketball stuff. Can you imagine if you're Keaton Wagler, right now? The Clippers' No. 5 pick in the 2026 draft was not sucked into the vortex of NBA's punishments because — and if there's a silver lining for the Clippers, it's this one — the league's investigation took so damn long that it wasn't able to levy the punishment in time to bar the Clippers from being able to draft the Illinois phenom in the lottery.

At the trade deadline, the Clippers traded Ivica Zubac and Kobe Brown to the Indiana Pacers for Bennedict Mathurin, Isaiah Jackson, the 2026 first-round pick (protected 1-4 and 10-30), a future 2029 first-round pick and a second-round pick. As part of the punishments, Wagler can play, but the 2029 pick acquired in the deal is gone and won't be returned to the Pacers, Zach Lowe reported.

It's not clear how the Raptors picks that were agreed to be sent to LA in the Leonard deal will be handled. The Clippers were set to receive the Raptors' 2031 and 2033 first-round picks in the transaction, but the NBA has stripped the Clippers of their picks in 2029 through 2033. We'll see how the NBA rules on the Toronto draft capital.

A year ago, in light of the investigation and possible punishments that the NBA could issue, I suggested that the Clippers should trade their future first-round picks for star players. Doing so would make it trickier for the NBA to hand out punishments as they chase a championship. If the Clippers mortgaged their future and traded their draft capital for say, now-traded stars like Giannis Antetokounmpo, Jaylen Brown and LaMelo Ball, how could the NBA pull them off the floor? Would they vacate a championship, if it came to that?

Instead, the Clippers shockingly went the other way and shed stars in order to add first-round picks. They traded Leonard, Zubac and James Harden. And now they have neither stars nor (many) picks.

But they do have Wagler, who is the point guard of the Clippers' very bleak future. Even though the 19-year-old didn't ask for any of this, he stands as the only Clippers first-round pick the team will stand to have for the foreseeable future, and he'll have to carry that weight throughout his tenure with the asset-bankrupt Clippers.

Not many tears will be shed for Wagler, who will make about $10 million in his rookie season to play professional basketball. But like Anthony Davis in the Luka Dončić trade, players often unfairly bear the fallout of their bosses' forsaken decisions. Davis didn't last in Dallas long, but the future of the Clippers is in Wagler's hands way more than it was yesterday. Though Darius Garland and Brandon Ingram are the placeholder stars that will suit up for the Clippers next season, Wagler is the innocent bystander that will be burdened by the Clippers' lack of future firepower.

If you thought this was the end of the Kawhi Leonard scandal, don't hold your breath. It should be mentioned that the NBA's statement brought to light a very significant detail: "The NBA and the NBPA have entered into an agreement confirming these penalties are final and binding on all parties."

Case closed! Right? Not so fast. The NBPA isn't going to fight this ruling and Leonard is accepting the fine, but the Clippers ostensibly have another "avenue" to pursue: court — and not the basketball one.

We'll see if the Clippers decide to fight this in America's judicial system. In doing so, Ballmer would be following in the footsteps of his predecessor. After Silver banned Donald Sterling for life after a racist recording was made public, Sterling sued the league for damages exceeding $1 billion, saying the league's punishments were "draconian."

A federal judge dismissed Sterling's suit in 2016.

There's another precedent I should raise here. In the Joe Smith fallout, the NBA did eventually return two first-round picks back to Minnesota for its subsequent good behavior. The big difference though is that Glen Taylor accepted the league's punishment and played nice. The Clippers, through Wednesday's red-hot comments, very much are not accepting the league's penalty.

Maybe Ballmer will learn Sterling's lesson and decide not to bring a lawsuit against the NBA. Then again, it's clear he didn't learn his original cap circumvention lesson from 2015 and here we are.

articles.title: Los Cavaliers harán su pretemporada NBA en España: se instalarán en el "Santuario" creado por Calderón y Berni Rodríguez
articles.standfirst: The Embassy es un complejo deportivo, "un santuario del rendimiento", diseñado y desarrollado José Manuel Calderón y Berni Rodríguez en Fuengirola (Málaga)
articles.summary: The Embassy es un complejo deportivo, "un santuario del rendimiento", diseñado y desarrollado José Manuel Calderón y Berni Rodríguez en Fuengirola (Málaga)
articles.body: Los Cleveland Cavaliers instalarán su campamento de entrenamientos en España, y prepararan su pretemporada para afrontar el curso NBA en 'The Embassy' de Fuengirola (Málaga) del 30 de septiembre al 5 de octubre. Las dos últimas temporadas los Cavs realizaron sus entrenamientos de pretemporada en la IMG Academy de Sarasota (Florida). "El campamento de entrenamiento es donde se sientan las bases de la temporada, y 'The Embassy' ofrece a nuestros jugadores, entrenadores y personal un entorno excepcional para comenzar esa labor", explicó Koby Altman, presidente de operaciones de baloncesto de los Cavaliers, en declaraciones que reproduce 'basketnews'. Altman reconoció que "las instalaciones se han consolidado como un referente para el talento y el rendimiento del baloncesto de élite; contar en nuestra organización con José Manuel Calderón convierte esto en una oportunidad especialmente única para nuestro equipo". José Manuel Calderón, que jugó en los Cavaliers 2017-2018, participó en el diseño y desarrollo de 'The Embassy' junto a Berni Rodríguez (ex de Unicaja y selección española). Manuel Escobar, director ejecutivo de The Embassy, también celebró la decisión de los Cavaliers de trasladar su preparación de pretemporada a España. "Recibir a los Cleveland Cavaliers en The Embassy para su concentración de entrenamiento es un honor enorme y un momento significativo para todos los que formamos parte de la organización. Que una organización de la NBA elija The Embassy como lugar para iniciar su temporada es un claro reflejo de esa visión», declaró Manuel Escobar, director ejecutivo de The Embassy.

articles.title: La NBA, contra la octava persona más rica del mundo
articles.standfirst: Los Clippers y su propietario, Steve Ballmer, han sido sancionados por saltarse el límite salarial pagando a Kawhi Leonard con contratos con otras empresas
articles.summary: Los Clippers y su propietario, Steve Ballmer, han sido sancionados por saltarse el límite salarial pagando a Kawhi Leonard con contratos con otras empresas
articles.body: Los Clippers han recibido una durísima sanción por saltarse el límite salarial ayudando a Kawhi Leonard a conseguir dinero más allá de su contrato para jugar al baloncesto. Se han quedado sin cinco primeras rondas del draft, una por año entre 2029 y 2033, la franquicia tendrá que pagar 30 millones de dólares y varios de sus ejecutivos han sido suspendidos de todas las actividades de la competición. Entre ellos, el propietario Steve Ballmer. La NBA se ha atrevido a hacer lo que muchos pensaban que no haría: ir contra uno de los mayores millonarios del mundo. Ballmer, de 70 años, fue director ejecutivo de Microsoft y, según Forbes, es la octava persona más rica del planeta con más de 150.000 millones de dólares. Para hacerse una idea, la suma de las fortunas de los 10 siguientes propietarios más adinerados de la NBA no llega a la que posee él. Después de estudiar en Harvard, fue contratado por la empresa informática en 1980. Íntimo amigo del fundador Bill Gates, acabó siendo presidente en 1998 y dos años más tarde ocupó el lugar de su colega como director ejecutivo. Permaneció en el cargo hasta 2014. En ese tiempo, triplicó las ventas y duplicó los beneficios de la compañía pese a pronósticos errados como el que hizo sobre los iPhone: "No hay ninguna posibilidad de que consiga una cuota de mercado significativa". Años después prohibió a su familia utilizar cualquier aparato de Apple. Al abandonar Microsoft, el dueño de los Clippers se llevó consigo una buena cantidad de acciones de la empresa, lo que le sigue generando enormes beneficios y le han llevado al Top 10 de la lista de Forbes. Con el dineral que posee se compró la franquicia por 2.000 millones, una cantidad irrisoria ahora viendo lo que se paga por los equipos de la NBA. Llegó tras no haber cuajado la adquisición de los Sonics y los Kings junto a un grupo de empresarios. En Los Ángeles, aprovechó su ocasión con la escandalosa salida en 2014 de Donald Sterling, el antiguo propietario, que tuvo que irse después de realizar comentarios racistas. En 2020, una encuesta realizada por 'The Athletic' situaba a Ballmer como el mejor propietario de una franquicia de la NBA. Un dueño comprometido y un aficionado más que se desgañita durante los encuentros, dispuesto a invertir hasta en la construcción de un pabellón, el modernísimo Intuit Dome, que es capaz de atraer a estrellas como Kawhi Leonard... Pero fueron las operaciones bajo cuerda para enriquecer al jugador lo que hace tiempo manchó la imagen de Ballmer. El periodista Pablo Torre destapó hace un año los pagos de la empresa Aspiration, con la que el alero tenía un contrato, aunque nunca realizó ningún trabajo a cambio. Ahora, después de una investigación independiente llevada a cabo por un prestigioso bufete de abogados, los Clippers y sus directivos han sido sancionados. Si se repitiera la encuesta sobre los mejores propietarios de la NBA, Ballmer estaría lejos de la cabeza por este escándalo que ha atentado contra uno de los principios básicos de la competición como es el límite salarial. Ballmer se defendía entonces diciendo que había sido estafado. Costaba creer que al octavo hombre más rico del mundo, rodeado de economistas, abogados y asesores, le hubieran engañado. Ahora, tras conocerse la sanción, los Clippers se oponen rotundamente a ella y rechazan "enérgicamente los hallazgos de la NBA, que son el resultado de una investigación fuertemente sesgada". Según el convenio colectivo de la competición, no caben recursos de amparo. Su única salida sería acudir a la justicia ordinaria. Dinero tienen de sobra para contratar a los mejores abogados.

articles.title: What happens next for the Clippers after NBA punishment? Steve Ballmer, Kawhi Leonard fallout explained
articles.summary: NBA News: The Los Angeles Clippers have been hit with one of the NBA’s most severe punishments in recent memory after a year-long investigation into the team’s .
articles.body: The Los Angeles Clippers have been hit with one of the NBA’s most severe punishments in recent memory after a year-long investigation into the team’s dealings with Kawhi Leonard uncovered what the league called a “pattern of misconduct” involving salary-cap circumvention.The fallout is enormous. The Clippers have been ordered to forfeit five first-round draft picks, fined $30 million, and placed under a five-year NBA compliance and monitoring program. Owner Steve Ballmer has been suspended from all league and team activities for one year, while President of Business Operations Gillian Zucker and President of Basketball Operations Lawrence Frank have also been suspended.Leonard himself was fined $700,000, while his uncle and former business manager, Dennis “Uncle Dennis” Robertson, has been banned from conducting business with NBA teams and their affiliates for five years.But what exactly did the Clippers do, and how did the Kawhi Leonard scandal startThe controversy centered on how Leonard was allegedly able to receive off-court income while playing for the Clippers. The NBA's investigation, conducted independently by law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, concluded that the Clippers did more than simply sign Leonard to an NBA contract.According to the league, the organization actively helped create additional income opportunities for Leonard through companies that already had business relationships with the Clippers.Four companies were identified: Aspiration Partners, Boingo Wireless, Daktronics and Lockton Insurance. The NBA said the Clippers initiated opportunities between Leonard and those companies and facilitated endorsement agreements between them.That distinction matters because NBA teams are not allowed to circumvent the collectively bargained salary-cap system by effectively providing players with additional compensation outside their contracts.The Aspiration deal became the biggest red flagThe investigation became public after reports surrounding Leonard's relationship with Aspiration, an environmental-finance company that has since gone bankrupt.Reports alleged that Leonard had a four-year, $28 million endorsement agreement with Aspiration despite doing little or no conventional endorsement work for the company.That immediately raised questions because Aspiration had a close financial relationship with Ballmer. The NBA subsequently opened its investigation into whether the arrangement was being used to provide Leonard with compensation outside the Clippers' salary structure.The league ultimately found that the issue went beyond Aspiration.According to the NBA, the Clippers had affirmatively initiated off-court income opportunities involving Leonard and four companies doing business with the franchise. The league also concluded that the Clippers induced companies to enter those arrangements by offering them business from the team.In other words, the NBA's finding was not simply that Leonard had outside endorsement deals.It was that the Clippers themselves were involved in creating and facilitating those opportunities, making them potentially part of an effort to provide Leonard with benefits beyond his NBA compensation.What did Steve Ballmer allegedly do?Ballmer, the billionaire Clippers owner, was not accused merely of being unaware of what his organization was doing.The NBA specifically suspended him for one year for knowingly seeking to help Leonard obtain off-court income opportunities.The league said Ballmer approved a business deal that he knew was a precondition for Aspiration to enter an endorsement agreement with Leonard. It also faulted him for failing to create conditions that ensured the organization followed the NBA's salary-cap circumvention rules.That finding put the franchise's owner directly at the center of the scandal.What role did Gillian Zucker play?Gillian Zucker, the Clippers' president of business operations, received a one-year suspension without pay.The NBA said Zucker was “primarily and directly culpable” for the impermissible endorsement arrangements.Even more seriously, the league said she provided false and misleading statements to investigators during the probe.Her punishment therefore wasn't simply about being part of the organization while the alleged conduct happened. The NBA concluded that she had a direct role in the arrangements themselves.What did Lawrence Frank do?Lawrence Frank, the Clippers' president of basketball operations, received a six-month suspension without pay.The NBA found that Frank was involved with the impermissible endorsement arrangements and approved expenses incurred by Leonard and his family that the league determined were not permitted.His suspension was shorter than Ballmer's and Zucker's, but his involvement still contributed to the league's conclusion that the violations were institutional rather than the actions of a single rogue employee.Where does “Uncle Dennis” come in?Dennis Robertson, better known as “Uncle Dennis,” was Leonard's uncle and former business manager.According to the NBA, Robertson made improper solicitations for off-court income opportunities on Leonard's behalf. The league also said the Clippers failed to report those solicitations.The NBA responded with perhaps the strangest punishment in the case: Robertson is banned for five years from conducting business or otherwise engaging with NBA teams and their affiliates on behalf of, or concerning, any player, employee or other league or team personnel.What did Kawhi Leonard do?Leonard was not suspended, but he was not cleared either.The NBA concluded that Leonard violated the salary-cap circumvention rules through Robertson's conduct on his behalf.The league said Leonard pressured the Clippers to assist him in obtaining off-court income opportunities, successfully obtained those opportunities, and failed to reimburse payments made by the Clippers for personal expenses.As a result, Leonard must pay the NBA $700,000.Leonard, however, said he entered his Clippers contract and the agreements in question in good faith and had no knowledge that anyone intended to circumvent the salary cap. He accepted responsibility for what he described as lapses in judgment by people within his inner circle.Why is the salary cap issue so serious?The NBA's salary cap exists to keep teams operating within a collectively bargained financial system.A team cannot simply give a player additional compensation through another channel because it cannot fit the player's desired compensation into the team's salary structure.That is why the distinction between a legitimate endorsement deal and an improper arrangement matters.A player can obviously make money away from basketball. But if a team helps arrange an outside deal with one of its business partners in order to provide the player with additional benefits connected to his relationship with the team, the league can view that as an attempt to circumvent the salary-cap system.That is essentially what the NBA says happened with Leonard and the Clippers.Steve Ballmer isn’t done fighting yet: What happens next after NBA punishes Clippers?The most damaging penalty may not be the $30 million fine.The Clippers will lose their first-round picks in 2029, 2030, 2031, 2032 and 2033.That strips the franchise of five consecutive first-round selections and potentially compromises its ability to rebuild through the draft for years.The team will also operate under an NBA-supervised compliance and monitoring program for five years.The NBA and NBPA have agreed that the penalties are final and binding, although the Clippers have made clear they intend to fight the findings through arbitration.The Clippers have rejected the league's conclusions.In a statement, the organization said it “vehemently reject[s]” the NBA's findings and argued that the investigation was biased and driven by a predetermined narrative.The team also claimed that what the league communicated privately differed from what it announced publicly and said it would challenge the findings and penalties through every available avenue.That means the story is not necessarily over.The NBA has delivered its verdict, but the Clippers are preparing to contest it.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: La jugadora que puede hacer el primer mate en un Mundial: "Es como Wembanyama"
articles.standfirst: La pívot Dominique Malonga (20 años, 1,98 metros y 2,16 de envergadura) aspira a hacer lo nunca visto en el torneo
articles.summary: La pívot Dominique Malonga (20 años, 1,98 metros y 2,16 de envergadura) aspira a hacer lo nunca visto en el torneo
articles.body: El Mundial Femenino que arranca este viernes en Berlín puede ver un acontecimiento histórico: el primer mate en la historia del torneo. Quien puede conseguirlo es Dominique Malonga, pívot francesa de 1,98 metros y 2,16 de envergadura. Lo ha hecho en muchos entrenamientos y también en partidos. Machaca desde los 14 años y ahora, con 20 años, es la más joven en firmar un mate durante un All Star de la WNBA. También lo hizo en un encuentro con la selección gala durante el PreMundial. “No son jugadas planeadas. Surgen en el momento. Es algo que llevo dentro y para mí es algo natural. Si se presenta la ocasión adecuada, no hay razón para no hacerlo", asegura la jugadora, compañera de Awa Fam en las Seattle Storm. En el All Star recibió una asistencia y culminó un contraataque. Con Francia, recuperó un balón y se lanzó hacia el aro rival. Las reacciones de sus compañeras y de los aficionados ante sus mates suelen ser de algarabía y locura. "Aportan mucha alegría y emoción al juego", asegura Malonga, "muy orgullosa de poder hacerlos". Porque a lo largo de la historia no han sido tantas las jugadoras profesionales capaces de colgarse del aro durante partidos: Lisa Leslie fue la primera en la WNBA, Liz Cambage lo hizo unos Juegos... Entre las españolas, la internacional Laura Nicholls los hacía en los entrenamientos y también la joven Sara Okeke, una de la mayores promesas del baloncesto español. "Es como Victor Wembanyama en el baloncesto femenino", la definió el histórico Tony Parker, que la fichó para su ASVEL Villeurbanne. Evidente comparación por su tamaño y su nacionalidad. La pívot es una de las razones por las que Francia podría plantar cara a Estados Unidos durante el Mundial. En cuestión de físico, son dos selecciones parejas. En la final olímpica de París en 2024, las galas ya dieron un susto a las grandes favoritas, quedándose a un paso de una campanada histórica: 67-66. "Esa es la razón por la que tenemos tanta confianza de cara a este Mundial, por lo que demostramos en 2024. Hay muchísima expectación, pero tampoco queremos confiarnos. Sabemos que queda mucho por hacer, pero estamos preparadas y hemos trabajado muy duro. Podemos ser aún mejores que entonces", afirma la jugadora nacida en Camerún e hija de exjugadores. Francia no ha conseguido una medalla en un Mundial Femenino desde la primera edición, allá por 1953, cuando se colgó el bronce. Ahora es aspirante al podio y la gran candidata a acabar con la dictadura de Estados Unidos en torneos a nivel planetario. "Tengo muchísimas ganas de salir a la cancha. Tenemos un gran equipo y estoy deseando ver lo que podemos lograr", afirma Malonga. Una medalla aliñada con un mate en los próximos días serían el premio completo.

articles.title: Los Clippers declaran la guerra a la NBA... y Kawhi se acerca a Toronto
articles.standfirst: El conjunto angelino rechaza en un durísimo comunicado las acusaciones y llevarán a los tribunales a la liga. La no suspensión de Leonard acelera su vuelta a los Raptors
articles.summary: El conjunto angelino rechaza en un durísimo comunicado las acusaciones y llevarán a los tribunales a la liga. La no suspensión de Leonard acelera su vuelta a los Raptors
articles.body: La NBA ha sacudido a Los Angeles Clippers con una sanción histórica tras un año de investigación por la presunta transgresión del límite salarial en torno a Kawhi Leonard. El castigo incluye cinco primeras rondas del Draft, una multa de 30 millones de dólares para la franquicia y la suspensión de un año para su propietario, Steve Ballmer, además de sanciones a varios ejecutivos. Leonard, por su parte, ha sido multado con 700.000 dólares, pero no ha sido suspendido. Los Clippers han respondido con enorme contundencia y han rechazado frontalmente las conclusiones de la NBA. “Rechazamos categóricamente las conclusiones de la NBA, que son el resultado de una investigación sumamente parcial que busca justificar una versión preconcebida en lugar de basarse en hechos y pruebas”, asegura la franquicia, que considera que el proceso no cumplió con las garantías de imparcialidad exigidas. El club de Los Ángeles anuncia además una batalla legal para defender su posición: “Durante el último año, hemos cooperado plenamente y de buena fe, y ahora lucharemos con la misma determinación para demostrar nuestra inocencia”. Los Clippers aseguran que “tenemos la intención de impugnar enérgicamente estas conclusiones y sanciones por todos los medios a nuestro alcance” y reclaman un arbitraje “ético e imparcial”. En medio del terremoto, la sanción puede tener una consecuencia inmediata en el futuro de Kawhi Leonard. La investigación mantenía paralizado el acuerdo entre los Clippers y los Toronto Raptors para el regreso del alero a Canadá. Al no haber sido suspendido Leonard, el principal obstáculo para completar la operación desaparece, y según informa Shams Charania en ESPN el traspaso podría hacerse efectivo en los próximos días. El regreso tendría un enorme componente sentimental y deportivo. Leonard volvería a Toronto, donde en 2019 conquistó el primer y único anillo de la historia de los Raptors, siendo además MVP de las Finales. Aquel fue su segundo campeonato, después del logrado con San Antonio en 2014, también con el premio al mejor jugador de las Finales. El acuerdo inicial contemplaba la llegada de Leonard a Toronto a cambio de Brandon Ingram, Gradey Dick y dos primeras rondas del Draft. Ahora la sanción puede cambiar las condiciones del intercambio. Los Clippers han perdido cinco futuras primeras rondas y podrían intentar exigir más activos a Toronto para compensar el golpe recibido. Los Raptors, sin embargo, tienen un poderoso incentivo para cerrar el acuerdo: recuperar al jugador que los llevó a la cima de la NBA. Después del terremoto provocado por la sanción, todo apunta a que el regreso de Kawhi a Toronto está más cerca que nunca.

articles.title: 4 NBA players who can win Rookie of the Year
articles.summary: Which of these 4 players will take home the honor?
articles.body:
Winning Rookie of the Year can be a great indicator of what a player's career might look like. While there have been some flops, most Rookie of the Year winners go on to have successful NBA careers. Winning the award requires more than talent. A player needs an opportunity, consistent production, and, most importantly, the trust of their franchise.

The 2026 NBA Draft may have been the most loaded draft class in over a decade, but only a few have the combination of talent and opportunity to emerge as favorites. Here are four rookies with the best chance to win Rookie of the Year.

Jun 23, 2026; New York, NY, USA; Draft prospect Darryn Peterson poses for photos on the red carpet before the 2026 NBA draft at Barclays Center. Mandatory Credit: Brad Penner-Imagn Images

Peterson is likely in one of the best situations to win the award.

He joins the Utah Jazz, a roster with impressive defenders and scorers from the forward position to center. Utah lacks a primary ball-handler and scorer, putting Peterson in position to take on that role.

Peterson is currently projected to start for the Jazz. Utah also has guards Keyonte George and Ace Bailey. George had an impressive season last year, while Bailey's rookie year was nothing to write home about. If Peterson can play alongside George as the primary scorer, there's no reason he shouldn't be a front-runner for Rookie of the Year.

Jun 23, 2026; New York, NY, USA; The fourth pick in the 2026 NBA draft, North Carolina forward Caleb Wilson after he was selected by the Chicago Bulls at Barclays Center. Mandatory Credit: Brad Penner-Imagn Images

Caleb Wilson was selected fourth overall by the Chicago Bulls. Chicago has Josh Giddey, Matas Buzelis and recently signed Norman Powell, but Wilson should still have plenty of opportunities.

Wilson arguably outperformed every other rookie in this year's draft class, making Chicago fans excited for the upcoming season. He should get opportunities to score, facilitate, and defend the rim. Chicago hasn't found their "guy" yet, and Wilson could prove himself as that player.

Jun 23, 2026; New York, NY, USA; NBA commissioner Adam Silver announces the eleventh pick in the 2026 NBA draft, Michigan forward Yaxel Lendeborg after he was selected by the Golden State Warriors at Barclays Center. Mandatory Credit: Brad Penner-Imagn Images

Lendeborg is the lowest-drafted player on this list, but he'll have plenty of opportunity to shine. He showcased his ability to score, playmake, rebound and defend during Summer League, making him one of the most versatile players in the class.

He joins the Golden State Warriors, who lack a primary scorer outside of Stephen Curry. With Jimmy Butler recovering from his ACL tear, the window is open for Lendeborg to take on a larger role.

Jun 25, 2026; Washington, DC, USA; Washington Wizards first round draft pick and number one overall pick AJ Dybantsa poses for a photo with his jersey during a press conference at InterContinental Hotel. Mandatory Credit: Amber Searls-Imagn Images

This list had to include the No. 1 overall pick.

Dybantsa joins the Wizards, who are loaded with talent. That could hurt his chances more than it helps, as he could be overshadowed by Trae Young and Anthony Davis.

Regardless, Dybantsa had an impressive Summer League, showcasing his scoring ability and elite athleticism. If he's trusted with a key role in Washington, he could make some noise in the Rookie of the Year race.

articles.title: ‘Set the Team Back to the Dark Ages’ – Clippers Broadcasting Legend ‘Stunned’ As NBA ‘Cracks Down’ on Kawhi Leonard Scandal
articles.summary: As the fallout from the Kawhi Leonard salary cap scandal continues to shake the league, legendary Clippers broadcaster Ralph Lawler expressed shock over the...
articles.body:
As the fallout from the Kawhi Leonard salary cap scandal continues to shake the league, legendary Clippers broadcaster Ralph Lawler expressed shock over the NBA's unprecedented penalties.

Lawler warned that losing five first-round draft picks sets the franchise back to the 'dark ages' while noting that Leonard surprisingly escaped the lightest.

Clippers Icon Ralph Lawler Points Out How Historic NBA Penalty Hurt Those Involved, But Kawhi Leonard 'Got Off Lightest'

Years after pulling off one of the biggest acquisitions in franchise history, the Clippers' championship dream has officially dissolved into a nightmare. What was supposed to be a golden era centered around Leonard has culminated in one of the NBA's most serious salary-cap circumvention cases.

Rather than lifting trophies, the organization is left picking up the pieces of the NBA's investigation, which found a pattern of misconduct and multiple significant violations.

At the center of the fallout was a $28 million side endorsement deal with green finance company Aspiration that served as off-the-books compensation, coupled with under-the-table perks tied to three other team sponsors.

When independent investigators wrapped up their yearlong probe, the verdict was damning. League Commissioner Adam Silver levied a historic $30 million fine on the Clippers, the heaviest financial penalty ever imposed on an NBA team.

Steve Ballmer, the billionaire owner, was hit with a full one-year ban from all team and league activities. President of Business Operations Gillian Zucker received a one-year unpaid suspension, while President of Basketball Operations Lawrence Frank received a six-month unpaid suspension.

Moreover, the Clippers were stripped of five future first-round draft picks spanning from 2029 through 2033.

As the sports world processed the magnitude of the punishment, no voice carried more weight within the fan base than Lawler's.

Lawler served as the "Voice of the Clippers" for 40 years before retiring in 2019. Having called games through decades of painful losing streaks, the vibrant "Lob City" era, and the team's eventual transformation into a big-market contender, Lawler knows the franchise and its staff better than almost anyone.

Taking to X, Lawler expressed sheer disbelief at how harshly the league cracked down:

"Stunned by the NBA crack down on the LA Clippers! Aside from Kawhi, I knew the punished parties well. Their lives are changed forevermore. Leonard got off lightest of the group. The 5 lost draft picks set the team back to the dark ages. Wow!"

Lawler's reaction hits on the most painful truth for Clippers faithful: the massive gap between who created the mess and who actually suffers from it.

For the two-time NBA champion, the personal cost is light. He was fined $700,000, a minor dent for a max-contract star, and completely avoided a playing suspension. He also blamed "lapses in judgment" by his manager and uncle, Dennis Robertson, who was hit with a five-year NBA ban.

With the league's investigation wrapped up, Leonard's trade back to the Toronto Raptors was unfrozen, letting him walk away without missing a single game on the court.

The Clippers and their fans, on the other hand, are left holding the bag. Even though the team released a statement saying they "vehemently reject" the league's findings and plan to contest the penalties, the reality on the ground is grim.

With top leadership sidelined, an almost empty draft war chest through 2033, and their franchise player gone, Clippers fans are staring down the exact "dark ages" Lawler warned about.
